title: What do American liberals & conservatives think about moderates? US study finds out
summary: A US study of 3,272 participants finds that political moderates are often treated as an out-group by partisans, who view them as aiding the opposing side. The "moderate as out-group" effect arises when issues are moralized and opponents are perceived as threatening, which can increase polarization and weaken incentives for compromise.
content:
New Delhi: Political moderates often seek a middle ground on contentious issues, rejecting extreme views from both the Left and the Right. But this may have made them enemies on both sides of the political spectrum, according to a new study by the American Psychological Association.

The research, published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: General on 27 July, involved five online experiments with 3,272 people in the United States. Participants were asked about their views on polarizing topics such as the Israel-Palestine conflict, abortion, and the 2024 US presidential election. While moderates expressed openness to opposing views, many partisans nonetheless perceived them as aiding the other side.

In one experiment conducted just days before the 2024 US election, respondents evaluated a hypothetical person who expressed support for both Donald Trump and Kamala Harris in polls. Participants were also asked whether the opposing candidate's victory would pose a threat to themselves, someone they know, or society. Those who perceived a threat were more likely to view the hypothetical moderate as an ally of the opposing camp.

"Democratic systems rely heavily on compromise, negotiation and coalition building, and moderates are often seen as the 'glue' that helps bridge ideological divides," said lead researcher Giulia Maimone, a postdoctoral scholar in marketing at the University of Florida. "If moderates are rejected by both sides, compromise itself may begin to look suspicious or disloyal."

Another experiment presented participants with a moderate policy allowing abortions in the first trimester. Researchers observed that both supporters and opponents of abortion interpreted the policy as supporting the opposing side. The team labelled this phenomenon the "moderate as out-group" effect.

"We find that the 'moderate as out-group' effect occurs when sociopolitical issues are moralized and, at the same time, the opposing side is perceived to be a threat to oneself, close ones, or society at large," the researchers wrote. They also noted that the effect is strongest when a moderate position is framed as pro-both sides and is attenuated when framed as pro-neither side.

Maimone warned that categorizing moderates as members of the opposing camp can exacerbate polarization: feeling rejected by both major camps may push moderates to ultimately choose one side. She suggested reducing moralized language around controversial debates and avoiding demonization of political opponents so they appear less threatening, which could make political cooperation seem more acceptable.

The study raises concerns about the social dynamics that can undermine compromise in democratic societies. If moderates are widely perceived as aiding adversaries, the normal incentives for negotiation and coalition-building may be eroded, with implications for how political discourse and policy debates are conducted.

The research adds to a growing literature on polarization by showing how perceptions, threat assessments, and moralized framing interact to shape who is included or excluded from political in-groups. Addressing these psychological and communicative dynamics could be an important step toward reducing hostile polarization and restoring some social space for compromise.
